crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: High-Frequency Market Microstructure
children.blurb: High-frequency market microstructure is the study of how trades actually happen at the finest timescales, from the arrival of an order to its execution or cancellation.

children.name: Non-Linear Factor Models
children.blurb: Non-linear factor models extend the linear factor framework by allowing a factor's effect on returns to depend on other factors, on the level of the factor itself, or on the market regime.

children.name: Learning Trade Execution
children.blurb: Learning trade execution is the use of machine learning to decide how, when, and where to place orders in financial markets.

children.name: Statistical Arbitrage
children.blurb: Statistical arbitrage is a quantitative trading approach that looks for relative value between related securities, often using statistical models to identify temporary mispricings.

children.name: Detecting Market Regime Shifts
children.blurb: Detecting market regime shifts is the practice of identifying when the statistical character of a market changes, for example from calm and trending to volatile and mean reverting, or from broad correlation to dispersion.

sections.body: Quantitative trading is the practice of using data and computation to decide what to buy, sell, and when, rather than relying on a person's judgment alone. Artificial intelligence enters this field through models that learn patterns from order books, price histories, news feeds and alternative data, then translate those patterns into positions. In market microstructure, learning systems estimate short term price pressure and liquidity from the stream of quotes and trades. Factor models use machine learning to combine many weak signals into a single expected return, and execution algorithms learn how to work a large order without moving the price against themselves. Statistical arbitrage systems hunt for temporary mispricings across related instruments, while regime detection models try to notice when the market's underlying behaviour has changed. None of this is theoretical, these methods run inside hedge funds, prop firms and bank desks every trading day.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The honest picture is mixed. Execution learning is the most settled area, because the objective is narrow and the feedback is fast, and many desks now use learned policies alongside older rule based schedules. Factor models have absorbed non linear methods, but the gains over well built linear models are often modest and fragile, and overfitting remains the central failure mode. Statistical arbitrage still works in some markets and decays quickly once others find the same signal, so capacity and crowding matter as much as accuracy. Regime shifts are recognised as real and important, yet detecting them in real time is unsolved, most methods either lag the change or fire on noise. Nothing here is guaranteed, past performance does not carry forward, and any claim of reliable prediction should be treated with suspicion.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages are arranged from the fastest timescale to the slowest. High-Frequency Market Microstructure is the foundation, covering the order book mechanics and data that everything else depends on, and it is where a reader should start to understand what the models actually see. Non-Linear Factor Models moves up to the daily and weekly horizon, showing how many signals are combined into forecasts and where overfitting creeps in. Learning Trade Execution sits between signal and market, and a reader goes there to understand how an order is worked once a decision has been made. Statistical Arbitrage shows how these pieces combine into a strategy that seeks relative mispricings rather than outright direction. Detecting Market Regime Shifts is the widest lens, addressing the question of when a model that worked yesterday should be distrusted today, and it is best read after the others because it reframes all of them.
